summaries.example: Imagine finding a toy in a dark room. You might turn your head, move closer, and run your fingers over it. Each action gives you new information. Some philosophers think action is not only a way to get information but also part of how seeing and sensing work.
summaries.summary: Action-based theories of perception ask how bodily movement and the ability to act relate to seeing and sensing. It is obvious that actions can help us gather information: turning around changes the view, and moving a hand across an object reveals its texture and shape. The stronger philosophical claim is that perception may depend on action in a deeper way. Berkeley argued that vision gains its sense of distance and solid shape through learned connections with touch and movement. Critics noted that vision can resist touch, as when a flat painting still looks three-dimensional, and that some animals guide movement visually very early in life. Later theories focused on eye movements and signals from the body. Some say the brain uses movement signals to keep the world looking steady when the eyes move. Others say perception depends on learning how movements change sensations. The entry also discusses theories in which perception is partly prepared action, and theories that connect spatial meaning with skills for acting in relation to objects. The theories differ, but they share the idea that perception may be more active than simply receiving pictures from the world.
key_ideas: Moving can change what we see, hear, or feel, so action can help us learn about the world.
Some theories say action is only a tool for getting new sensory information. Other theories say action is part of perception itself.
George Berkeley argued that touch and movement help vision seem three-dimensional, but later thinkers raised objections.
Later theories study eye movements, learning, special glasses, and devices that turn sights into touches.
Philosophers disagree about how closely seeing and acting are connected.
summaries.why_it_matters: This topic helps explain ordinary experiences such as catching a ball, judging distance, keeping the room steady while looking around, and learning to use unusual visual equipment. It also shows how philosophy and psychology can work together: philosophers clarify what perception means, while experiments test how movement, touch, eye signals, and learning affect experience.

important_terms.definition: Getting information through seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, or other senses.
Something your body does, such as turning your head, reaching, walking, or moving your eyes.
Information about where something is compared with your own body: above, below, near, far, left, or right.
A view that says seeing depends partly on knowing how your movements change what you sense.

questions_to_think_about: Do you understand an object better when you move around it?
Could you see depth and distance without ever touching or moving toward things?
If glasses changed where things appeared, would practice change what you perceived?
Is seeing mainly receiving information, or does it involve preparing to act?

summaries.example: Suppose you look at a mug while moving your eyes from its handle to its rim. The image on each retina shifts, yet the mug normally appears to stay in place. One proposal says the visual system compares incoming retinal changes with a copy of the eye-movement command. Another says it preserves a few attended landmarks and checks their locations after the saccade. These explanations agree that eye movement matters, but they disagree about the mechanism.
summaries.summary: Action-based theories challenge the idea that perception is simply an input process followed by an output response. The entry accepts an uncontroversial starting point: action changes sensory stimulation. Turning, walking, touching, and moving the eyes can reveal information that would otherwise remain unavailable. The philosophical question is whether this dependence is merely instrumental or whether perceptual content itself depends on action-related capacities. Early theories, especially Berkeley's, held that vision acquires depth through learned associations with touch and movement. Critics argued that visual experience can remain three-dimensional when touch conflicts with it, and that visual guidance may occur without the proposed tactile education. Lotze and Helmholtz then used movement-related signals to explain how locations are organized within the visual field; Lotze emphasized kinaesthetic feedback, while Helmholtz emphasized motor commands. Twentieth-century sensorimotor theories proposed that perception requires knowledge of the sensory effects of self-generated movement. Work on visual stability, prism adaptation, inverted images, and sensory substitution supported some action-sensitive explanations, but also created difficulties: adaptation can occur with passive movement or even without motor action, and its endpoint may involve recalibrated proprioception rather than a transformed visual field. Enactive theories make sensorimotor knowledge central to world-presenting perception, while critics question whether two-dimensional perspectival properties are perceptually basic and whether vision and action are really so tightly unified. Motor-component theories instead claim that eye-movement signals and proprioceptive feedback combine with visual input. Mod
key_ideas: The entry distinguishes instrumental dependence of perception on action from constitutive dependence, in which action-related capacities help make perceptual content possible.

Berkeley treated touch and movement as educating vision about depth; objections include visual capture, problems for association, and evidence that vision can be spatially effective without prior tactile training.
Lotze and Helmholtz extended action-based explanations to the two-dimensional organization of the visual field, disagreeing about whether local signs come from sensory feedback or motor outflow.

Sensorimotor theories explain perception through predicted sensory consequences of movement, but experiments on optical rearrangement do not clearly show that active movement is always necessary for adaptation.
Readiness theories range from the modest claim that covert action planning can alter perception to the bold claim that perception is a form of action readiness.

Evans and Grush argue that spatial content depends on a network linking sensory inputs, bodily information, and detailed possibilities for behavior, without simply reducing perception to muscle activity.
summaries.why_it_matters: The debate matters because it concerns what perception is, not just how people move. It connects philosophical questions about perceptual content with empirical questions about eye movements, neural signals, learning, sensory substitution, and visual illusions. It also clarifies several different meanings of 'embodied': perception might use bodily signals, depend on learned movement-sensation relations, be altered by action planning, or acquire spatial meaning within a larger perception-action network. Keeping these possibilities distinct prevents the broad claim that perception is 'active' from becoming too vague.

important_terms.definition: A philosophical view that action, or capacities for controlling action, helps constitute perceptual experience rather than merely supplying new sensory input.
A framework in which movement changes sensory input, while perception depends directly on the resulting input; action is useful but not constitutive.
The problem of explaining why objects appear stable even though their retinal images shift during eye movements.
A signal copied from a motor command and used to compare expected sensory change with actual sensory input.
The view that perception depends on learned knowledge of regular links between movements and their sensory consequences.
A theory claiming that perceptual states involve, or are identical with, readiness to perform suitably directed actions.
A theory on which sensory inputs and behavioral dispositions jointly form a system that gives spatial content to experience.
Information about the body's position and movement, including signals from muscles and joints.

questions_to_think_about: If a person adapts to reversed or displaced vision, has vision changed, bodily position sense changed, or both?
Does the ability to predict sensory consequences explain perception, or only surprise when predictions fail?
Can a visual experience have spatial content if the observer cannot perform the associated action?
Are conscious visual experience and visually guided motor control separate systems or deeply connected ones?
What would count as evidence that action is constitutive of perception rather than merely helpful to it?

summaries.example: Try walking toward a friend while looking at a tree beside them. As you move, the tree seems to shift relative to the friend, while the friend may stay in roughly the same direction. Your movement changes the visual pattern reaching your eyes, but it also helps you judge distance and position. An action-based philosopher asks whether movement is just helping you collect clues or is part of what makes the scene spatially meaningful.
summaries.summary: Action-based theories of perception examine the connection between sensing the world and moving within it. Actions plainly provide useful information: walking changes the pattern of light reaching the eyes, moving around an object reveals new sides, and running a hand over a surface reveals texture and shape. The more controversial claim is that action is involved in perception in a constitutive way, meaning that action-related abilities help determine what perceptual experience represents. Berkeley's early theory held that sight begins with light and color and gains its apparent depth through learned connections with touch and movement. Critics argued that vision can remain powerful when it conflicts with touch, and that vision can guide behavior before such learning seems possible. Later thinkers studied local signs and the role of eye movements in organizing visual direction. Modern theories often focus on sensorimotor contingencies: the regular relationships between movements and their sensory results. An efference copy may help explain why the world seems stable during eye movements. Reafference and enactive theories extend this idea to broader perception, claiming that perceivers learn the sensory consequences of their own movements. Yet prism and inversion experiments show that adaptation can sometimes occur without active movement, leading some researchers to emphasize information about conflicts between vision and body position. Other theories say motor signals help determine apparent direction, distance, size, or motion, while readiness theories say hidden action planning can influence what we perceive. key_ideas: Actions can reveal information by changing our viewpoint or by letting us touch, track, or approach things.
The central disagreement is whether action merely changes sensory inputs or helps constitute perceptual experience.
Berkeley connected visual depth with learned links between sight, touch, and movement, but critics pointed to visual capture, animal behavior, and difficulties with learning by association.
Lotze and Helmholtz proposed different kinds of movement-related signals to explain how the visual field gets organized.
Sensorimotor theories use prediction: a perceiver learns what sensory changes normally follow self-made movements.
Experiments with prisms, inverted images, and sensory-substitution devices provide evidence for learning and plasticity, but they also challenge the idea that active movement is always required.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding this debate helps explain why perception changes when people move, practice, use unusual lenses, or receive information through a new sense. It also shows why one label can hide several different claims. Saying perception is action-based might mean that action gathers evidence, that the brain predicts movement-related sensations, that motor preparation changes appearance, or that spatial meaning depends on skills for interacting with the environment. Separating these claims makes both the philosophical arguments and the experimental evidence easier to evaluate.

important_terms.definition: The process by which a person or animal obtains information through the senses.
A bodily movement or behavior, including eye movements, walking, reaching, or touching.
The regular way a particular movement changes sensory input.
A motor signal sent with a copy that can help the brain predict the sensory result of movement.
The tendency for the visual world to seem steady even when eye movements shift the image on the retina.
A theory saying that perception involves knowing how movement will change sensory stimulation.
Information about the position or movement of body parts, especially through muscles and joints.

questions_to_think_about: Why does a room usually look stable when you move your eyes quickly?
Would practice with vision-changing glasses alter your visual experience, your sense of body position, or both?
Does touching an object teach vision about its shape, or can vision work independently?
What is the difference between knowing what movement will cause and being ready to make a movement?
Can a person with very limited movement still have normal spatial perception?
